def: A blood test showing average blood glucose over about three months, given as a percentage. Under 5.7% is the normal range.
Sugars and syrups put into food during processing or at the table. Sugar naturally present in whole fruit and plain milk is not included.
A recommended daily amount of a nutrient, set when there is not enough evidence for a precise requirement. Water and fibre targets are adequate intakes.
Movement that raises your heart rate and breathing for a sustained time, such as brisk walking, cycling or swimming.
The energy your body uses at complete rest to stay alive, usually 60 to 70% of what you burn in a day.
The force of blood against artery walls, written as systolic over diastolic in mm Hg, for example 118/76.
Weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. A quick screening measure of weight for height.
A paced breathing pattern: breathe in, hold, breathe out and hold again, each for four counts.
The time your body takes to clear half the caffeine from a dose: about 5 hours in most adults, with wide variation.
The unit of energy used for food and activity. Food labels show kilocalories, commonly just called calories.
One of the three macronutrients, found in grains, fruit, vegetables, pulses and sugars. It provides 4 kcal per gram.
A fatty substance carried in the blood. LDL is the type linked with artery disease; HDL helps carry cholesterol away.
Your internal 24-hour clock, set mainly by light, that times sleep, alertness, hormones and body temperature.
The bottom number in a blood pressure reading: the pressure in arteries while the heart rests between beats.
The parts of plant foods your body cannot digest. It supports bowel health, blood sugar control and cholesterol.
An A1C result translated into the same units a glucose meter shows.
The WHO term for added sugars plus the sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice.
A ranking of how quickly a carbohydrate food raises blood glucose compared with pure glucose.
The gap between your maximum and resting heart rate. The Karvonen method sets training zones as percentages of it.
Bands of heart rate, usually five, that describe how hard you are working.
Packaged products made mostly from refined ingredients and additives, such as soft drinks, sweets, crisps and many ready meals.
The medical name for persistently high blood pressure: 130/80 mm Hg or higher under U.S. guidelines, 140/90 in many other countries.
A way of setting heart-rate zones using your resting heart rate as well as your maximum.
Everything in your body that is not fat: muscle, bone, organs and water.
The nutrients you need in large amounts: protein, carbohydrate and fat.
The fastest your heart can beat during all-out effort. It falls with age and is often estimated as 208 minus 0.7 times age.
Metabolic equivalent of task. One MET is the energy used sitting quietly; brisk walking is about 4.3 METs.
A widely used formula that estimates resting energy needs from weight, height, age and sex.
Effort at which you can talk but not sing, roughly 3 to 6 METs.
Exercise that makes muscles work against resistance: weights, bands, body weight or heavy manual work.
The heaviest weight you can lift once with good form. Often estimated from a lighter set.
A measure of smoking history: packs smoked per day multiplied by years smoked.
Blood glucose higher than normal but below the diabetes threshold, for example an A1C of 5.7 to 6.4%.
A macronutrient built from amino acids, needed to build and repair tissue. It provides 4 kcal per gram.
Recommended Dietary Allowance: the daily intake that meets the needs of nearly all healthy people.
Your pulse when calm and rested, usually 60 to 100 beats a minute in adults and lower in fit people.
A type of fat found mainly in fatty meat, butter, cheese, and coconut and palm oils. Guidelines advise keeping it under 10% of calories.
A test for a disease in people with no symptoms, done to catch it early.
Waking time spent sitting or lying down with very low energy use.
A roughly 90-minute pass through light, deep and REM sleep. Most adults complete four to six a night.
The habits and bedroom conditions that support good sleep.
The part of salt that affects blood pressure. One teaspoon of salt contains about 2,300 mg.
A national measure of alcohol. It is 14 g of pure alcohol in the U.S., 13.45 g in Canada, 10 g in Australia and 8 g (one unit) in the UK.
The top number in a blood pressure reading: the pressure in arteries when the heart beats.
Total daily energy expenditure: everything you burn in a day, from resting needs to movement and digestion.
An industrially produced fat that raises heart-disease risk. Many countries have banned or restricted it.
A condition in which the body does not use insulin well and blood glucose stays too high.
Fats found in olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado and oily fish. Replacing saturated fat with them lowers LDL cholesterol.
A scale of the strength of sunburn-causing ultraviolet light. Protection is advised at 3 and above.
Effort at which you can say only a few words without pausing for breath, 6 METs or more.
The maximum rate at which your body can use oxygen during exercise; a measure of aerobic fitness.
Waist measurement divided by height. Keeping it under 0.5 is linked with lower health risk.
Grains that keep all three parts of the kernel, such as oats, brown rice, whole wheat and barley.
Easy aerobic effort, roughly 60 to 70% of maximum heart rate, at which you can hold a conversation.
